content.chiefComplaint: Extreme dizziness and 'feeling like I'm going to pass out' since this morning.

historyPhysical.hpi: 78-year-old female brought in by daughter. Patient reports waking up feeling 'woozy' and unable to stand without support. Describes sensation as 'lightheadedness,' denies room spinning (vertigo). Reports two episodes of 'greying out' while sitting for breakfast. Denies chest pain or shortness of breath. Daughter notes patient has been more confused than baseline.
historyPhysical.familyHistory: Mother had stroke at 80. Father had MI at 70.

physicalExam.cardiovascular: Profoundly bradycardic, regular rhythm, variable intensity S1 (Cannon a-waves)
physicalExam.neurological: GCS 14 (Confused), CN II-XII intact, no nystagmus

nursesNotes.author: RN Triage
nursesNotes.entry: Patient presents with complaint of severe dizziness. States she feels like she is going to faint. Skin is cool and pale. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. Radial pulse is thready and very slow. Monitor applied immediately showing HR in 30s. Patient placed on stretcher.

nursesNotes.author: RN Primary
nursesNotes.entry: Dr. Attending at bedside. 12-lead EKG obtained showing P waves dissociated from QRS complexes. Transcutaneous pacing pads applied to chest/back as a precaution. IV access established in right AC.

orders.order: Atropine 1mg IV Push x1 PRN for symptomatic bradycardia
Hold all AV nodal blocking agents (Beta Blockers/CCB)

radiology.findings: Atrial rate 88 bpm. Ventricular rate 32 bpm. No relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. QRS duration 140ms (wide).

screening.interpretation: Unable to perform due to severe hypotension/dizziness while supine.

rationale.coreConcept: Differentiation and management of dizziness caused by unstable cardiac arrhythmias (Third-Degree Heart Block).
rationale.caseSummary: 78-year-old female presents with presyncope (lightheadedness) and profound bradycardia (HR 30s). The dizziness is a symptom of cerebral hypoperfusion due to low cardiac output. The cause is Complete Heart Block, requiring pacing.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Symptoms of 'dizziness' must be categorized: Vertigo (Vestibular) vs Presyncope (Cardiovascular/Perfusion) vs Disequilibrium (Neuro). This patient has Presyncope signs (hypotension, pallor, bradycardia).
rationale.trap: Confusing 'dizziness' with 'vertigo'. This patient does not have room-spinning sensation; she has low flow state.
rationale.goldenRule: Unstable Bradycardia (Hypotension + AMS) requires Electricity (Pacing), not just Drugs.

steps.description: Interpret ECG: P waves dissociated from QRS = 3rd Degree Block.
Apply pacing pads and prepare to pace.

mnemonic.title: PACE
mnemonic.content: P-Pads on, A-Atropine (try), C-Consult Cardio, E-Electricity (Transvenous)

cheatSheet.title: Heart Block Types
points: 3rd Deg: Ps and Qs don't agree (Deadly).

referenceInfo.anatomy: AV Node and Bundle of His.
referenceInfo.physiology: In 3rd degree block, no atrial impulses reach ventricles. Ventricles beat at intrinsic rate (20-40 bpm), which is often insufficient to maintain Cardiac Output (CO = HR x SV).
referenceInfo.pharm: Atropine works at the SA/AV node. It may not work in 3rd degree block if the escape rhythm is infra-nodal (wide QRS).

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Recognize that 'dizziness' in the elderly is often a cardiac sentinel event.
recommendedActions: Check pulse immediately for any complaint of dizziness.

screens.prompt: Click to highlight the findings that indicate hemodynamic instability requiring immediate intervention.
screens.text: The nurse assesses the patient. She reports feeling lightheaded. Vital signs show blood pressure 82/48 mmHg and heart rate 32 bpm. Patient is slow to respond to questions. Skin is pale and cool. She states she forgot her reading glasses. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. She has chronic knee pain.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient has HR 32 and hypotension. This is 'Unstable' by ACLS definitions.
rationale.answerAnalysis: BP 82/48 (Hypotension), HR 32 (Severe Bradycardia), Slow to respond (Altered Mental Status), Pale/Cool skin (Poor perfusion), Cap refill 4s (Poor perfusion). Lightheadedness is a symptom, but the *signs* of instability are the vitals/exam. Glasses and knee pain are irrelevant.
rationale.trap: Thinking HR 32 is acceptable in an athlete. In a 78-year-old with AMS, it is critical.

steps.description: Determine if rate is the cause of the instability.

mnemonic.title: CASH
mnemonic.content: C-Chest pain, A-Altered Mental Status, S-Short of breath, H-Hypotension

referenceInfo.physiology: MAP < 60-65 mmHg reduces Cerebral Perfusion Pressure, leading to confusion and syncope.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Prioritize the finding that kills the fastest: Hypotension + Bradycardia.
recommendedActions: Get the pacer pads ready immediately.

screens.prompt: For each finding, indicate if it is consistent with Complete Heart Block, Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), or Acute Stroke.

rows.text: Room-spinning sensation triggered by head movement

rationale.caseSummary: Dizziness is a vague term. Specific cues point to the etiology.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Heart Block: HR < 40, Presyncope (low flow), AV dissociation. BPPV: Room spinning (Vertigo), Nystagmus. Stroke: Focal neurological deficits (Face droop).
rationale.trap: Assuming 'dizziness' implies stroke in the elderly. Check the heart rate first!
rationale.goldenRule: Vertigo = Room spins. Presyncope = Patient spins/fades out.

steps.description: Match vitals to the sensation (Bradycardia matches Presyncope).

mnemonic.title: ATTEST
mnemonic.content: A-Associated symptoms, T-Timing, T-Triggers, E-Exam (Neuro/Cardiac), S-Sugar (Hypoglycemia), T-Trauma

referenceInfo.physiology: Inner ear crystals (otoconia) cause BPPV. Electrical block causes Heart Block.
referenceInfo.pharm: Meclizine treats BPPV dizziness but worsens Heart Block (anticholinergic effects/sedation).

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: If the patient is pale/hypotensive, it is rarely just 'vertigo'.
recommendedActions: Obtain 12-lead EKG for all 'dizzy' elderly patients.

screens.prompt: Drag the nursing priorities into the correct order for this unstable patient.

rationale.caseSummary: Unstable patient (Hypotensive/AMS). Safety net (Pads) comes before drugs.
rationale.answerAnalysis: 1. Pads (Safety net first - can be done while IV is started, but is priority for survival). 2. IV access (Needed for drugs). 3. Atropine (First line drug, though may not work in 3rd degree). 4. Transvenous Pacing (Invasive, takes time, definitive bridge). 5. Education (Last).
rationale.trap: Giving Atropine before putting pads on. If Atropine fails (likely in 3rd degree), you need the pacer *now*.
rationale.goldenRule: Pads on Patient. Before Pushing Meds.

steps.description: Atropine is a bridge, Pacing is the destination.

cheatSheet.title: Atropine Dosing
points: Ineffective in Mobitz II and 3rd Degree Block.

referenceInfo.physiology: TCP delivers current through chest wall to depolarize myocardium. Requires high current (mA).
referenceInfo.pharm: Atropine blocks vagal tone. 3rd degree block is often below the AV node, where vagal tone has less influence.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Don't delay electricity for an IV line. Pads go on in seconds.
recommendedActions: Turn pacer on to 'Demand' mode immediately.

screens.prompt: Complete the diagram: Select actions, the condition, and parameters to monitor.

rationale.coreConcept: Definitive management of Complete Heart Block.
rationale.caseSummary: Patient has AV dissociation and hemodynamic instability. Requires pacing and holding rate-slowing meds.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Condition: 3rd Degree Block. Actions: Pace (definitive treatment for instability), Atropine (attempted bridge), Hold Beta Blockers (removing the cause/exacerbating factor). Epley is for BPPV. tPA is for Stroke. Parameters: Capture (is the pacer working?), MAP (is perfusion adequate?), Mental Status (is brain perfused?).
rationale.trap: Selecting 'Sinus Bradycardia'. Sinus Brady implies the P waves drive the QRS. Here they are dissociated.
rationale.goldenRule: In Pacing: Electrical Capture (Spike + Complex) does NOT equal Pulse. You must feel for Mechanical Capture.

steps.description: Need to increase rate to increase Cardiac Output.

cheatSheet.title: Pacing Thresholds
points: Dial up Current (mA) until capture seen.

referenceInfo.physiology: Electrical depolarization (QRS) causes Calcium release -> Muscle Contraction. In dying hearts, you can have electrical activity without contraction (PEA).
referenceInfo.pharm: Sedation/Analgesia is required for TCP if patient is awake (it hurts!).

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Sedate the patient if BP allows. TCP is painful.
recommendedActions: Use femoral pulse to check capture (avoids muscle twitch confusion).

screens.prompt: Complete the nursing understanding of pharmacology.
screens.text: The nurse recognizes that Atropine may be ineffective because the blockage is likely located at the %{d1}, requiring %{d2} as the priority intervention.

options.text: AV Node or Bundle of His (Infra-nodal)

rationale.coreConcept: Limitations of Atropine in High-Degree Blocks.
rationale.caseSummary: Understanding why we don't just rely on drugs for this patient.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Atropine works by inhibiting the Vagus nerve (Vagolytic), which innervates the SA and AV nodes. In 3rd degree block with wide QRS, the escape rhythm is ventricular (Infra-nodal), below where the Vagus nerve reaches. Therefore, Atropine often does nothing. Pacing is the only way to drive the ventricles.
rationale.trap: Thinking Atropine fixes all slow heart rates.
rationale.goldenRule: Wide QRS Bradycardia = Atropine likely fails. Go to Pacing.

steps.description: Vagus nerve doesn't reach distal ventricles.

mnemonic.title: Wide-Wait-Pace
mnemonic.content: Wide QRS? Wait on Atropine? No, Pace.

referenceInfo.physiology: Parasympathetic (Vagus) innervation decreases as you go down the conduction system. Ventricles have minimal vagal control.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Look at the QRS width. Narrow? Atropine might work. Wide? Probably not.

screens.prompt: Which findings indicate the pacing is effective and the patient's status is improving? Select all that apply.

options.text: Palpable femoral pulse matches the set pacer rate
Monitor shows pacer spikes followed by wide QRS complexes
Patient complains of chest discomfort with each impulse

rationale.caseSummary: Ensuring the machine is actually saving the patient.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Palpable pulse matching rate = Mechanical Capture (Essential). Mental status/BP improvement = Perfusion success. Spikes + QRS = Electrical Capture. Chest discomfort is a side effect/expected finding of TCP (muscle contraction), not a sign of 'improvement' or 'effectiveness' of the cardiac output itself (it's actually a nuisance finding we treat with sedation).
rationale.trap: Selecting chest pain. While it confirms current is being delivered, it's not a sign of *clinical improvement*.
rationale.goldenRule: Electrical Capture is on the screen. Mechanical Capture is on the pulse.

mnemonic.title: SPIKE
mnemonic.content: S-Spike visible, P-Pulse palpable, I-Improved BP, K-Kidneys (urine), E-Extremities warm

cheatSheet.title: Checking Capture
points: Don't use carotid (muscle twitch mimics pulse).
Use Pulse Oximetry waveform (if good signal).

referenceInfo.physiology: TCP stimulates pectoralis muscles (pain/twitch) AND heart muscle. Sedation is humane.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Always confirm mechanical capture. Electrical capture alone does not generate blood pressure (PEA).
